title: The rank-one cubic relation gives Gauss identities in an affine group
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $H$ an affine group scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}A$, meaning an affine scheme with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams, as in [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Write $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$ and $\mathbf G_m(R)=R^\times$ for every commutative $A$-algebra $R$. Suppose $x:\mathbf G_a\to H$ and $d:\mathbf G_m\to H$ are group-scheme homomorphisms and $h\in H(A)$ satisfies, on all such $R$,
$$d(t)x(u)d(t)^{-1}=x(t^2u),\quad h d(t)h^{-1}=d(t^{-1}),\quad h^2=d(-1),\quad(hx(1))^3=1.$$
Define $y:\mathbf G_a\to H$ by $y(v)=h x(-v)h^{-1}$. For every $R$ and $u,v\in R$ with $w=1+uv\in R^\times$, one has
$$x(u)y(v)=y(v/w)d(w)x(u/w),\qquad y(v)x(u)=x(u/w)d(w)^{-1}y(v/w).$$
One also has $h=x(1)y(-1)x(1)$. All equations are identities of scheme morphisms on their indicated domains, including the domain $\operatorname{Spec}A[u,v,(1+uv)^{-1}]$ for the two Gauss identities. No invertibility of $u$ or $v$, characteristic restriction, reducedness or Noetherian assumption is imposed.

proof.text:
Use the group-scheme operations of [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Thus $x(a+b)=x(a)x(b)$, $x(-a)=x(a)^{-1}$, and the same formulas hold for $y$, since it is conjugation of $x(-v)$. Also $d(ab)=d(a)d(b)$. The torus relations give
$$d(t)y(v)d(t)^{-1}=h d(t^{-1})x(-v)d(t)h^{-1}=y(t^{-2}v).$$
Here $d(t)h=h d(t^{-1})$, obtained from the assumed conjugation by $h$. These are equalities over every $A$-algebra, with only $t$ required to be a unit.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4, equations (6.2.2)--(6.2.4), printed pp.201--203: agent-supplied explicit rank-one calculation omitted in the source. No SGA source used.

proof.text:
Put $X=x(1)$ and $z=h^2=d(-1)$. Since $(-1)^2=1$, the torus action says that $z$ commutes with every $x(a)$, and $z^2=1$; as a power of $h$, it also commutes with $h$. From $(hX)^3=1$ one gets $XhXhX=h^{-1}$. Therefore
$$x(1)y(-1)x(1)=XhXh^{-1}X=z^{-1}XhXhX=z^{-1}h^{-1}=h,$$
the last equality following from $h^4=z^2=1$. This proves the Weyl-element assertion over $A$ and after every base change.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4, equations (6.2.2)--(6.2.4), printed pp.201--203: agent-supplied explicit rank-one calculation omitted in the source. No SGA source used.

proof.text: For subsequent equality reflection, write the affine scheme $H$ as $\operatorname{Spec}C$, using [def-pc-scheme]. The affine-spectrum correspondence [def-weil-affine-spectrum] identifies $H(R)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{A\text{-alg}}(C,R)$. If $j:R\hookrightarrow B$ is injective and two such maps become equal after composition with $j$, their values on each $c\in C$ were equal already. Consequently $H(R)\to H(B)$ is injective. This is coordinatewise cancellation, without a reducedness assumption. If $R$ is the zero ring, $H(R)$ is a singleton, so all assertions there hold automatically.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4, equations (6.2.2)--(6.2.4), printed pp.201--203: agent-supplied explicit rank-one calculation omitted in the source. No SGA source used.

proof.text:
Let $R$ be a nonzero $A$-algebra and $t\in R^\times$. Set $B=R[S]/(S^2-t)$ and let $s$ be the class of $S$. The monic-quotient basis of [lem-weil-pbc-monic-quotient-free], applied to this monic degree-two polynomial, gives the basis $(1,s)$. Hence $R\to B$ is injective: the coordinate of $r\cdot1$ along $1$ is $r$. Moreover $s$ is a unit with inverse $t^{-1}s$. Conjugate step 2 by $d(s)$ in $H(B)$, using step 1:
$$x(t)y(-t^{-1})x(t)=d(s)h d(s)^{-1}=d(s^2)h=d(t)h.$$
The penultimate equality uses $h d(s)^{-1}=d(s)h$. Step 3 reflects this equality back to $H(R)$. Thus, for every unit $t$, put $N(t)=x(t)y(-t^{-1})x(t)=d(t)h$. In particular
$$N(a)d(b)=d(b)^{-1}N(a)=N(a/b)\quad(a,b\in R^\times).$$

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4, equations (6.2.2)--(6.2.4), printed pp.201--203: agent-supplied explicit rank-one calculation omitted in the source. No SGA source used.

proof.text:
First suppose $v$ and $w=1+uv$ are units. The definition of $N(-v^{-1})$ in step 4 gives
$$y(v)=x(v^{-1})N(-v^{-1})x(v^{-1}).$$
Apply the same formula to $v/w$. Moving $d(w)$ past the adjacent $x$ by the assumed torus relation, and then using $N(a)d(w)=N(a/w)$, yields the explicit calculation
$$\begin{aligned}
y(v/w)d(w)x(u/w)
&=x(w/v)N(-w/v)x(w/v)d(w)x(u/w)\\
&=x(w/v)N(-w/v)d(w)x(1/(wv))x(u/w)\\
&=x(w/v)N(-1/v)x(1/(wv)+u/w)\\
&=x(u+1/v)N(-1/v)x(1/v)\\
&=x(u)y(v).
\end{aligned}$$
Here $w/v=u+1/v$ and $1/(wv)+u/w=1/v$. Every division displayed is legitimate under precisely the temporary assumptions that $v,w$ are units; $u$ need not be a unit.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4, equations (6.2.2)--(6.2.4), printed pp.201--203: agent-supplied explicit rank-one calculation omitted in the source. No SGA source used.

proof.text: Remove the temporary condition on $v$ universally. Put $P=A[U,V]$ [def-weil-polynomial-ring], $W=1+UV$, and $D=P[W^{-1}]$. Multiplication by $V$ on $P$ is injective: its coefficient at $U^iV^{j+1}$ is the original coefficient at $U^iV^j$. If $V(p/W^m)=0$ in $D$, the fraction equality in [def-weil-ring-localization-away] gives $W^nVp=0$ in $P$ for some $n$. Cancel $V$ to get $W^np=0$, which says $p/W^m=0$. Thus $V$ is a non-zero-divisor on $D$, and the same fraction criterion makes $D\to D[V^{-1}]$ injective. Step 5 proves the first identity in $H(D[V^{-1}])$ for $u=U,v=V$. Step 3 therefore proves it in $H(D)$. For any $A$-algebra $R$ and $u,v\in R$ with $1+uv$ a unit, the polynomial evaluation followed by [lem-weil-pbc-ring-localization-universal-property] defines $D\to R$, $U\mapsto u$, $V\mapsto v$, $W^{-1}\mapsto(1+uv)^{-1}$. Naturality gives the first identity in $H(R)$. Its equality in $H(D)$ is also the required equality of morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}D\to H$.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4, equations (6.2.2)--(6.2.4), printed pp.201--203: agent-supplied explicit rank-one calculation omitted in the source. No SGA source used.

proof.text:
In the first identity replace $(u,v)$ by $(-u,-v)$; its denominator remains $w=1+uv$. Invert both sides, using the additive-group inverse formulas from step 1. This gives
$$y(v)x(u)=x(u/w)d(w)^{-1}y(v/w).$$
The same operation on the universal equality over $D$ proves the second equality of scheme morphisms. Step 2 already proved the assertion about $h$. All displayed maps are built from $x,y,d,h$ and the group operations, with the only inverted function on the Gauss domain being $W$; hence every clause holds on its stated domain.
